text:
To understand how a refrigerator maintains the cold temperature of our food, we must first look at the concept of a refrigeration cycle, which is essentially a closed loop of heat transfer. Unlike a simple freezer that just removes heat, a refrigerator uses a cycle to move heat from the inside (where we are) to the outside (where the heat is dumped). This process relies on four main components: the compressor, the condenser, the expansion valve, and the evaporator. To keep the explanation detailed, we need to walk through each of these components and how they work together to keep our fridge cool.

The first component to consider is the compressor. Often, people think of the compressor as just a big motor, but it is actually the heart of the refrigeration system. The compressor is a mechanical device that compresses a low-pressure gas of refrigerant. When the compressor does this, it increases the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant gas. This high-pressure, high-temperature gas is then sent to the next component, the condenser. The compressor's job is to make the refrigerant "hot" and "high-pressure" so that it can release its heat to the outside environment. Without the compressor, the refrigerant would not have the energy needed to cool the interior of the fridge
